speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Chairman, I beg leave to move "that the total sum to be allocated for Head Q of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore has great ambitions to achieve a thriving digital economy and smart nation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In past Parliamentary debates, I argued that talent and data are, in my opinion, the most basic yet most important success factors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need data to innovate and we need people to get things done.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But along with new capabilities come new opportunities and challenges.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, vast amounts of data could be used to train Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve productivity and reduce human errors but it could perpetuate biases if we are not careful with the quality of data used.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Scale and speed of how information can get transmitted online help to share knowledge and impart new skills regardless of where the parties are and when, and perhaps even rally people to raise resources to help strangers or foreign countries in crisis.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But if misused, it can also propagate, extend and magnify harm to the innocent.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, legislation becomes a powerful tool to protect the vulnerable from harm online.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It can provide clarity to what is considered harmful, what recourse does a victim have and who should be responsible for what actions needed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And on responsibility, it is increasingly clear that protecting users is no longer just the responsibility of the Government or the individuals, but platforms too have gained the expertise and perspective over time to join the fight against online harms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, during the debate last year, I raised my concerns about having adequate protection in the Metaverse and the need for legislation and protection mechanisms to catch up with technological development.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must protect our people online just as we do in the real world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But in doing so, we also need to calibrate carefully so that we do not inadvertently suffocate innovation or over-burden well-meaning businesses wanting to scale and thrive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is also aligned to the spirit of Government's efforts in encouraging businesses to go digital in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, it is important for regulations and compliance to be clear in its objectives, streamline processes and paperwork so that whatever is needed to be done addresses the objectives on point, not more than what is needed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Otherwise, we risk hampering smaller enterprises' digitalisation journey and lose out further, because large enterprises are typically better resourced to meet these requirements.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, how do we balance data protection and data for innovation?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I will talk more about this in my other cut.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And in encouraging enterprises or individuals to digitalise and upskill through monetary incentives, we need to ask might the application or accountability process be so tedious such that they end up remaining in their comfort zones and stick to just being "good enough" and avoid digital transformation altogether?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could the MCI share more about its efforts in removing barriers and encouraging Singaporeans and enterprises to go digital?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Schemes such as Tech Pass, TechSkills Accelerator (TeSA), Professional Conversion Programme (PCP) help to boost tech talent supply.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Government expounding on the need for more tech talents and highlighting the specific profiles in demand serve to inform and influence students' decisions in what to major or specialise in.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Such "intervention" is useful as it helps to connect the industry and education and align the demand and supply.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The challenges and opportunities presented will require a wise and competent Government that can harness the power of technology to build Singapore while putting in place guardrails to protect our people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How then will the Government ensure a good balance between protection and facilitation?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What are the measures taken by our Government in countering cyber addictions, especially for youths and young children?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How can MCI play a part in equipping schools, parents and the community at large in raising awareness on the risks of cyber addictions and the methods of prevention?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Unfortunately, this has also left many elderly and less tech-savvy citizens behind.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What takes digital natives a few seconds to complete can be painfully difficult for some seniors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many struggle to come up with strong passwords and have difficulty typing them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Tapping a phone screen or double clicking a mouse poses dexterity challenges.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The solution, however, is not to run manual and digital services in parallel forever.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: That would negate the productivity benefits brought about by digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Instead, firms and Government agencies should provide in-person assistance to seniors to navigate their digital services.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can more ServiceSG centres be set up in every neighbourhood?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, how is the Government raising awareness among residents of their availability?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are private sector organisations like banks expected to provide such services for their less digitally savvy customers?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many seniors are already wary of using technology.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While seniors are not the only victims of scams, they tend to feel much more vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Their adult children, Government advertisements and the media are constantly sounding warnings to them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: That message has sunk in to such an extent that many of them avoid using digital services like Internet banking altogether, for fear of being scammed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, without Internet banking accounts, they will encounter many roadblocks in an increasingly cashless society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How is the Government tackling the challenge of getting seniors to embrace digital technology while also ensuring they are informed about basic precautions to avoid falling victim to scams?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Vulnerable groups are disproportionately affected by harmful online content which can include hate speech, cyberbullying, online harassment, disinformation, scams and fraud, and predatory behaviour.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Young people may be familiar with technology, using it every day but they may lack the maturity, life experiences and alertness to protect themselves.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The frequent exposure will also increase the opportunities for those with malicious intent.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Women can also be targeted with online harassment and abuse, including threats of violence, sexual harassment and revenge porn.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: People with disabilities may be targeted with online abuse and hate speech.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: They may also face barriers in accessing online content and services due to inaccessible web design and digital platforms.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: LGBTQ+ individuals are also at risk of being targeted with hate speech and discrimination online.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: This can lead to feelings of isolation and distress and can contribute to mental health issues, such as anxiety and depression.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: In 2020, I did an IG live chat with Keegan, a 19-year-old resident of mine who was undergoing hormone replacement therapy.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Keegan was brave enough to want to share his journey in gender transition and how his family had supported him.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: While there were many voices of encouragement for him, I understand that unfortunately, Keegan also experienced online hate speech and attacks.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Overall, harmful online content can have a significant impact on vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The groups span a wide spectrum and their challenges and needs could be very specific.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The Government should raise general awareness of these issues and take steps to protect vulnerable individuals from online harm.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It is also important to work with the respective communities and organisations which are familiar with the subject matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Both these documents were referred to by a writer in the bibliography of his book, "The History of the People's Action Party", which is now on public sale.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The National Archives said that they did not have the documents but that they were in the hands of the Ministry of Manpower (MOM).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, MOM replied to say that it does not, as a general policy, grant public access to Government files that have not been made public through the National Archives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It also said that Members of Parliament similarly do not have access to Government files and can seek information from the Government through a Parliamentary Question.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms He Ting Ru, take your two cuts together, please.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When we talk about building resilience as a nation, we should also avoid hindering the public's ability to scrutinise and deeply learn about our history so that we and our children may develop a more precise understanding and draw insights from it to formulate better decisions for the future.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, if declassification continues to be slow, is the Government using or working on one day using new tech, like, AI, to accelerate the process?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Why are these documents not automatically visible since they are already declassified?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This lowers the barriers for research and will foster a broader ecosystem on the study of our history.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Leader of the Opposition earlier spoke what the difficulties he faced when making requests to access certain Government files, despite the documents being made available to researchers previously.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Could we thus refine the request process to make clearer the mechanisms available to individuals who wish to appeal against rejections of their requests, by allowing an independent process by which the appeal is adjudicated?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This process can also take into account concerns about other decisions surrounding declassification issues.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When former Member for Aljunied GRC, Mr Low Thia Khiang, filed a cut on this topic in 2014, he noted that the 30-year rule was adopted by many countries, including the United Kingdom and Israel.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Mr Chairman, in today's interconnected world, state agencies, like other public facing entities and corporations need to conduct outreach.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singaporeans need and deserve timely accurate and useful information about public services, and also about the work that our Public Service does.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What Singaporeans are less informed about is the effectiveness of public relations, outreach and advertising campaigns, run by state agencies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Campaigns and actions run on public money should be accountable to the public, not just in terms of whether there is wrongdoing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is little indication that this is the case, but it is also about how the money is spent and how effective that expenditure is.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Recently, Singaporeans have also noticed prominent advertising campaigns relating to Ministry of National Development (MND)'s efforts to keep public housing affordable.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While public awareness and education efforts are necessary, these are still large sums of money.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It appears to be a missed opportunity here.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: MCI should assess the effectiveness of the various different campaigns and outreach programmes across Ministries into which Singapore puts our funds.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will give a better holistic view on how these programmes and campaigns are evaluated and thus adjusted to improve effects or, if necessary, cut for under performance.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What are the obstacles in either tracking the effectiveness of these campaigns or publishing reports of KPIs?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How else could we address the concerns above?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, fiscal prudence also means that we need to be able to maximise the bang for our buck, when it comes to spending public funds.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Instagram function to show that an IG post is sponsored was not used in that particular instance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For transparency, would the Government agree to have clear labels on all advertisements indicating the responsible agency?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: After all, political ads are required to have labels issued by the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation (POFMA) Office.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But some advertising seems to not embody a nudging intent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some ads seem to be aimed more at fostering "feel good" vibes towards an agency, and some even seem aimed at persuading the public to see the Government in a good light, with no clear public interest served in terms of ultimately nudging positive behaviours.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is an advertisement on the housing programme.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This ad, referred to by the hon members Mr Leong Mun Wai and Ms Hazel Poa earlier in this House, is aimed at persuading the public that, "We are committed to keeping HDB flats affordable and accessible for Singaporeans" and presents various factoids about Build-To-Order (BTO) launches and prices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But what is the public interest served here?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To raise awareness so people apply for BTOs?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The application rates for BTOs are already very high and rising.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, what behaviour exactly are we nudging with this ad?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, the ad seems more aimed at persuading people that the Government is doing a good job, keeping housing affordable and accessible, which is an opinion about public policy and one might say, politics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The latter is more akin to political advertising and should not be funded with public money.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, the practice of making false environmentally-friendly claims in advertising is dubbed greenwashing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore, it would seem that action is very rarely taken against advertisers who make dubious claims with the intent to deceive consumers that their products are "environmentally-friendly", "carbon neutral" and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, France's Climate Law prohibits companies from advertising that their products are carbon neutral, unless they can provide public information to back that up.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: South Korea's government is simplifying its process to fine companies that make false claims about environmental impact.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The UK government has created a Green Claims Code and done some enforcement around that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While what counts as greenwashing is not always clear, I would like to propose some solutions here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: First, our Singapore Code of Advertising Practice should explicitly cover greenwashing, with the Government developing legislation to bring clarity on what constitutes greenwashing in advertising.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE) and industry bodies can support this, with the Government playing an arbiter role and also taking reference from definitions found in laws overseas while adapting them locally.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: When ready, we can develop relevant legislation, which could include the mandatory provision of supporting documents for companies that choose to make green claims.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is an early adopter of initiatives to tackle greenwashing, which could provide lessons.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2022, MAS announced that funds that are sold to retail investors in Singapore under the label of meeting environmental, social, governance (ESG) standards will now have to back up their claims with new disclosure and reporting guidelines.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Aside from legislating and enforcing against false advertising under the Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act and sector-specific laws like the Estate Agents Act and the Medicines Act, much more also needs to be done on engaging the public to remind them that spotting and reporting potential offences is a public good and will benefit society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Engagement will also better help us understand what the key on-the-ground issues with greenwashing are, even as we eventually aim to legislate and enforce against greenwashing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, the advancement in technology has given rise to people accessing news online both from mainstream media as well as other sources.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Public funding is being provided to our local media organisations to enable them to better service audiences in a digital age.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What are our local media organsations doing to capture the attention of news readers online to retain and grow share?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the potential of harmful influences online, how are our local media organisations building and strengthening their capabilities to engage audiences online and to maintain trust, especially amongst younger demographics?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: But we must not inadvertently create a new inequality or widen the existing gap, between those who can access and exploit the new digital technologies, and those who cannot.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Our digitalisation efforts today are for the youths today and seniors tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: But we still have a generation of senior Singaporeans who struggle to keep up with the pace of digitalisation, despite everyone's best efforts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Therefore, I would like to ask: How has the Government progressed in ensuring Singaporeans have access and have the know-how to harness the benefits of going digital?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: What are the "wins" and opportunities for improvement?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Therefore, the Government should also design and proliferate solutions that connect seniors to the wider community, and design it in a way that is easy for them to use and not daunting.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: In the MacPherson constituency, we tried doing this with the MacPherson Care app.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: It has not easy, but we will continue to persevere.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: But we should also encourage such efforts across the nation too.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Therefore, I would like to ask: how will the Government encourage similar ground-up community initiatives to solve real life problems?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: As we continue on our journey towards digitalisation, information literacy is increasingly important.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: However, fake news, malicious falsehoods and scams continue to sprout, 就好像打不死的蟑螂.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: A whole-of-society effort is needed to combat misinformation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Educating the public on how to discern fake news and falsehoods such that it becomes a natural intuition is the best way to inoculate our population against the poison of falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Currently, there are lessons in school to raise awareness on online falsehoods and scams, but there is room to dive deeper and encourage greater critical thinking through quizzes and project work as students mature and advance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: That being said, adults are just as vulnerable – it is not easy to discern which information source is credible.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: What else is the Government doing to raise awareness of the importance of information literacy and educating the public to be discerning readers?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: At that time, it was technically a portable wireless telephone that people used for making calls and sending short messages (SMSes).

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Today, the mobile phone is a lot more than that.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: In fact, I do not think many people use their mobile phones just to make a call or send an SMS today.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We use it to check our social media, do our shopping, make our bank transfers, play games, take photos, among the many things that we multitask in modern day life.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The handheld device connects us to a whole digital world.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The spaces we can reach through digital means have become larger, as we perform almost all transactions, connect with anyone anywhere in the world, through a small screen at a fingertip.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: However, there are individuals in Singapore who find difficulty navigating a small screen.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Recently, I attended a session conducted by Infocomm Media Development Agency's (IMDA) digital ambassadors at Brahm Centre in Tampines.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: A mock-up grocery store was set up for senior residents to make purchases via e-payment.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The ambassadors were very patient and provided one-on-one service to show the seniors step by step.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: But I just hope that they will have the confidence to do e-payments in real life.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: However, I also noticed that some residents were still hesitant.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I remember years ago, when automated teller machines (ATMs) became available, it also took me a while to trust that the machine would dispense the right amount of money and update my bank account accordingly.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Imagine the apprehension of a much older person facing the digital world today.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Hence, I was heartened that Minister Josephine Teo spoke about the "Digital first, but not Digital-only" approach as a kinder and more appropriate position to take.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The Government will have to allocate some manpower resources to offer counter services, a hotline manned by a real person, process cheque payment and so on.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: (In Mandarin):   Digital services are becoming increasingly common in our society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: However, many seniors are still reluctant towards digital living.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: They are afraid of falling into online scam traps from inadvertently pressing a wrong button.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: While digital services carry certain risks, they also bring many conveniences.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: With a smartphone, we are able to know what is happening in the world and learn new knowledge without going out.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: In Woodgrove, I am very grateful to the team of digital ambassadors at the SG Digital Community Hub.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Prior to the upgrading of the Fuchun Community Club, they worked from 10 am to 6 pm daily to help our seniors, guiding seniors on a one-to-one basis to help them move towards digital living.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: During this period of time when our Community Club is under renovation, they continue to work closely with Citizens' Consultative Committee to go outdoors and set up digital assistance booths at a series of activities organised by the Woodgrove community, to encourage senior citizens to embark on a digital Journey.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Take for example the recent Community Emergency Preparedness Day held at 888 Plaza jointly organised with the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF).

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: The digital ambassadors present on that day encouraged our residents to download the SCDF's My Responder app which offers many benefits such as the location of the closest AED when someone needs CPR urgently.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The process must be paced to allow SMEs to understand how the transition will operate within the context of their business.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Assisting SMEs and heartland operators in this regard is key.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, the Digital for Life movement was set up to promote digital inclusion, encourage and support Singaporeans from all walks of life to embrace digital technologies to participate in the digital world and enrich their lives.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: An important aspect that the Digital for Life movement is to promote good digital habits which includes cyber safety, media literacy and how to manage risks and handle online harms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, I have had the good fortune of working with the teams at MCI and IMDA in the past as they developed the Digital for Life efforts, including the DfL Festival.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I can attest to the creativity and dedication of the teams in creating various meaningful platforms and opportunities for learning and collaboration, as we work to enhance digital literacy and capabilities within the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One of the beautiful things about the DfL effort is the community of partners that have been rallied to support digital empowerment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I brought my grassroots leaders to the DfL Festival at Heartbeat@Bedok last year and they were inspired by the array of programmes available for the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I must also mention that the digital ambassadors had joined us for many community programmes, creating awareness and providing support in digital empowerment for my residents at Bukit Batok East (BBE).

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is also value in thinking about good and thoughtful design of digital changes that allows for meaningful transition in a way that does not overwhelm those who are not digitally savvy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Former Nominated Member of Parliament, Prof Lim Sun Sun, shared her views in an article in The Straits Times last year about the lessons we could take from the design of the CDC vouchers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She mentioned the principle of skeuomorphism, where functions or objects in digital interfaces resemble their physical counterparts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This makes the digital interfaces more familiar to users, and to some extent more intuitive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: She lauded the design of the denominations of the vouchers and the consideration for the digitally less adept.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In fact, she said the thoughtful design may also help ease later adopters into accepting more advanced modes of digital payment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Indeed, the roll-out of the CDC vouchers was an opportunity for me to engage many of the elderly residents as well as the heartland shop owners on digital capability.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some of my elderly Bukit Batok East (BBE) residents would come to my community club office to get the print-out of the CDC vouchers but there were also some who sought to learn how to download the vouchers and use their phones to pay for their purchases We will continue to slowly build capability at different levels so that people do not feel left out and can also grow in this digitalisation process.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This journey needs to continue, not just for Bukit Batok East (BBE) but also the whole nation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is a lot more that we can do to ensure efforts are inclusive to address different needs and different capabilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With increased digitalisation and the future of work changing, our school-going children must acquire digital competencies that will ensure that they are ready for the future workplace.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure that our school-going children not only have access to hardware but are also digitally proficient?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In particular, how do we bridge the digital divide and ensure that children from lower-income families are not disadvantaged and will have the opportunity to develop their digital proficiency?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Through the efforts of MCI to grow the Information and Communications (I&C) sector and drive digital maturity, many firms have adopted digital technology.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: MCI has been developing the digital ecosystem and advancing digital utilities such as PayNow and Singpass and also providing support for broad-based enterprise digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond just adopting digital technology, how can we ensure that digitalisation enables Singapore to remain globally competitive even as businesses face rising costs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many businesses cite costs of implementation as a barrier to adopt digital technology.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do you assist companies to bring about cost savings from their digital investments?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For companies that have embraced digitalisation and want to further enhance their capabilities, how are we supporting them to do so?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Google parent, Alphabet, removed 12,000 of its employees.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Amazon shed 18,000 jobs and Salesforce axed 10% of its workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of the layoffs were due to economical uncertainty and aggressive overhiring during the tech boom years.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the volatility of the labour market as tech companies rationalise their operations, how are we ensuring that our tech workforce stays resilient, especially with the rapid evolution of technology?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, we live in an era of technological disruptions.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These disruptions are changing the way we live, work and interact with each other.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The way business has been conventionally conducted in industries such as retail and media are also being ruthlessly upended.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even in non-IT sectors, employers increasingly expect employees to possess adequate IT competencies.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For instance, it is not a stretch for organisations to expect employees to exhibit basic mastery in areas such as cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, an organisation's cyber defence is only as strong as its weakest link.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: An employee that succumbs to phishing emails, unintentionally introduces malware into a company's network, thereby opening the doors for corporate espionage or sabotage activities, would likely not be viewed upon favourably by his or her supervisors.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Employees may be expected to leverage technology in enhancing collaboration across teams at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Employers may increasingly expect employees to be proficient in using collaboration tools and platforms to work closely with their colleagues and business partners.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Employers may also expect employees to harness technology to innovate business processes, improve customer service experiences and enhance overall productivity.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we help Singaporeans grow relevant digital competencies such that they can keep up and stay ahead of the curve in a world of continuing technological disruptions?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How do we make "learning and adapting to ever-changing technologies" a way of life amongst our working population?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How do we help more senior members of our workforce manage the stresses of adapting to new technologies and tools?

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After all, it is only human for one to be anxious about the unknown and to fear making mistakes.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is particularly so in work environments such as in the healthcare industry, where any mistakes in the use of technology can result in grave consequences.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, digital transformation is a strategic imperative for all businesses in the new economy.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Over the past several years, the Government has partnered industry to drive "SMEs Go Digital" with pre-approved solutions, business grants as well as consultancy support.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: E-payment with PayNow was a lifesaver for businesses during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Can MCI update us on the progress of e-payment adoption as well as e-invoicing and e-signature?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In the most recent Singapore Business Federation (SBF) survey, businesses have called out that the lack of talent and know-how are barriers for SMEs to digitalise and transform.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister update us on how the implementation of CTO-as-a-Service has supported the SMEs with regards to digital leadership and know-how?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: TechSkills Accelerator (TeSA) and Career Conversion Programmes have focused on developing and reskilling local talent to meet the demands for information and communications technology (ICT) skills.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How successful have we been developing the required skills to meet our needs?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, how successful have we been in attracting strategic global tech talent with the ONE Pass programme?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I have heard positive feedback on the efforts made to make Budget 2023 simple to understand for the ordinary Singaporean and businesses.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: That said, what measures are in place to ensure that Government agencies do not spend on advertising on what can be perceived as self-promotion of the Government or to show it in a positive light?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How does MCI measure the effectiveness of its spending?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We have the highest average internet connection speed in Asia and the number of 4G subscriptions in Singapore is almost one and a half times that of our population.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: As coverage expands, how stable has 5G been and how will the Government help citizens and businesses to utilise and maximise the benefits that 5G can offer?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How will the Government partner the industries to create more use cases that will further propel our economy forward?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: As articulated in my cut to PMO last week, adequate data protection is most certainly necessary.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: But there is apprehension and perhaps confusion around the use of data and companies would understandably also be wary of sharing data stemming from competition concerns.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Thus, how can we avail and share data in a secure environment that allows experiments and product testing without compromising data privacy and security?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Could the Government play a greater role in working with industry players to facilitate this?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Given the rapid advancement of technology such as blockchain and cryptography, might there be scope for more curated Government data to be accessed in a safe, controlled and anonymous manner?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: As we look at 5G and the likes of Web 3.0 now, we must continue to look ahead and think of 6G, Web 4.0 and beyond.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: These require industry engagements, jointly imagining the future and charting out what infrastructure or building blocks are needed to enable that future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How will the Government partner the industries to co-imagine the future and build the digital infrastructure needed that is secure, versatile and green?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: It has made possible the high broadband penetration to households and businesses in Singapore and enables access to services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The pandemic has demonstrated the value of investing in the broadband infrastructure as the NBN has been instrumental in providing the connectivity for Singaporeans to work, learn and access services from their homes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With the acceleration and speed of digitalisation in Singapore and our Smart Nation ambition, the demand, volume and complexity of our infrastructure will grow exponentially.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What are our next steps and investments for the next generation of NBN to build capacity and high-speed connectivity for future needs, to realise potential opportunities and to be prepared for unexpected challenges?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Beyond capacity and speed of connectivity, security risks, privacy and environmental sustainability will also have to be key considerations as we plan for our future NBN.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted many businesses and demonstrated the importance of digital technology to enable businesses to continue to operate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: While businesses do understand the importance of transformation and digitalisation of their business, current economic conditions and rising business costs faced by businesses, especially SMEs, do pose challenges.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: There are a slew of initiatives and programmes to support businesses to digitalise, just to name a few – CTO-as-a-Service, Digital Leaders' Programme, Industry Digital Plans (IDP) and Advanced Digital Solutions (ADS).

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How have these programmes enabled businesses to digitalise, to seize opportunities and to raise their competitiveness?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, earlier in the debate, I outlined the lessons learnt from our Smart Nation journey as we strengthen our digital social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MCI plays a key role in overseeing this compact, ensuring that it remains robust amid technological disruption and that it benefits all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our theme for Committee of Supply this year is therefore "Empowering Singaporeans to thrive in our digital future".

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To do so, we must sustain the two aspects of our digital social compact: the aspirational and the protective.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our aspiration is for all Singaporeans to seize the opportunities created through digital developments.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To achieve this, we must build the foundational infrastructure to support our digital economy and society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Sound infrastructure planning has been a cornerstone of Singapore's success.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, the shape of our city for the next 50 years has been mapped in URA's Long Term Plan.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Land Transport Master Plan 2040 outlines our transport ambitions for the next two decades.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Few countries think this far ahead, much less organise themselves to realise such plans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To succeed in our digital future, we need an equally thoughtful and committed approach to digital infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This blueprint will lay out the full scope of our long-term infrastructural ambitions, cutting across broadband, mobile and Wi-Fi networks, as well as our undersea cables.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will lay the groundwork for us to transcend our resource constraints and create economic opportunities for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Given the fast-changing nature of digital, it would be unwise for Government to attempt this exercise on our own.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I have therefore asked Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary to co-chair an advisory panel comprising business and industry leaders, to bring them on board early and to make sure that our blueprint incorporates their needs.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I expect this phase of our work to take six to nine months.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Senior Minister of State Janil will outline the specifics of our plan.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Of course, it is not just infrastructure that must be primed for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our people and businesses must be ready too.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The importance of digitalisation is not lost on our businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ninety-three percent Singapore firms have adopted at least one digital technology and the demand for tech talent across the economy is strong.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But there are still areas where businesses face hurdles, especially as the global baseline of digital adoption rises and competition heats up.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will comprehensively lay out how we are promoting and supercharging digital transformation at the national, sectoral and firm levels.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How will share more about our plans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In pursuing our digital ambitions, we must not neglect the equally important protective dimension of our digital social compact: the dimension of trust and safety.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The path of digital development must be wide enough to accommodate as many as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Those who fall off this path will find it hard to support and participate in digital developments, much less embrace its benefits.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The second is about keeping digital technologies safe for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The digital realm has created opportunities for malicious actors to manipulate, deceive and coerce.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Compromise of our digital infrastructure and services could severely disrupt our economy and our lives.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Such occurrences breed a sense of danger and distrust.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The third concerns how we keep our society united and resilient.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We recognise the risk of digital technologies being exploited to undermine social cohesion through this misinformation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Left unaddressed, this can deepen fault lines, polarise societies and fuel intolerance as well as hatred.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, I will explain what MCI is doing to address these issues.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, on inclusion, which Ms Tin Pei Ling and Mr Sharael Taha have asked about.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In terms of connectivity, 92% of our households have access to a computer and 98% have broadband.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is far more than many countries can say.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, MCI believes we can reach a higher bar in terms of access as well as inclusion.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One group we remain concerned about are lower-income households.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For most households, digital connectivity has become as essential as water and electricity.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But for some, connectivity can still feel costly.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since 2020, we have helped over 46,000 households stay connected through the NEU PC Plus and Home Access schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will streamline these schemes into one, ease the application process and provide more affordable digital access for those who need it most.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will provide subsidised broadband and digital devices to eligible low-income Singaporean households.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Those living in 1- to 3-room flats will pay $10, while those in 4-room or larger flats will pay $15 monthly.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For another $5 monthly, they can double their bandwidth from 500 Mbps to 1 Gbps.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Households with students on MOE's Financial Assistance Schemes may also enjoy the highest level of subsidy depending on income.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will work with these agencies to auto-qualify these schemes' beneficiaries.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To achieve digital inclusion, broadband access must be accompanied by device access.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is often a bigger barrier as the costs are higher and harder to spread out.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For larger households with school-going children, we are partnering the people sector, through organisations like Engineering Good and SGBono, to provide up to 1,000 refurbished laptops per year to support them.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: From the demand seen in existing programmes, this number should be sufficient to meet current needs.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, allow me to describe the gist of our updated policy in Mandarin and how we should think about our seniors in our digital future.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will also outline what it means to be "digital first, but not digital only", which Mr Baey Yam Keng and Ms Janet Ang have asked about.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore has achieved very high levels of digital access amongst our households, to the envy of many nations.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: That said, digital access alone does not equate to digital inclusion.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, there are many seniors around us who own the latest handphone model but do not know how to use many of its functions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Hence, the Government is advocating for a "Digital First" and not "Digital Only" approach for now.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This means that we will continue to provide non-digital options for essential services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Many people have told me that this message was very reassuring, helping to ease their anxieties.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, some have also asked me if it means that our seniors no longer need to learn digital skills.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a matter of fact, the latest survey shows that the digital skills of seniors have improved over the past two years.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More seniors in their seventies or older are developing their digital proficiency, with the percentage rising from 7% to 29% -- an increase of 22%.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The data shows that our seniors understand that the digital future is materialising, and they should – and they can – adapt, just as they have successfully adapted to many aspects of Singapore’s modernisation in the past.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These figures, and the various ForwardSG citizen consultations, also show that we should not rush that process.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In imparting digital skills to our seniors, the learning process should consider their ability to absorb information and make good use of peers to support their learning.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The content should be in line with the practical needs of the seniors, such as teaching them e-payment.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The design of digital technologies should incorporate their perspectives and be intuitive for their use.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In other words, we should not underestimate the learning spirit or ability of our seniors.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: What they need is time, opportunity, encouragement, and empathy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Therefore, be it the Government, businesses, or community groups, let us help our seniors to pick up digital skills and be with them on this journey every step of the way.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (In English) Mr Chairman, let me emphasise this.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While some seniors need help with digital skills, we should not dismiss their ability to be part of our digital future.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: What they need are time, opportunity and empathy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Take Mr Richard Yip, a 72-year-old grandfather of three who discovered NLB's MakeIT programme through NLB's app.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members may recall that the MakeIT programme allows residents to experiment with fabrication technologies at libraries around Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Yip was intrigued by the 3D printing technology on offer at Jurong Regional Library.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: He started using it to print small solid pieces such as insects and dinosaurs, which his grandchildren loved and which made him incredibly popular with them.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Over time, Mr Yip progressed to using coding and robotic microcontrollers to create moveable toys for his grandchildren, making him even more popular.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: He is now an advocate for 3D printing, describing it as a "dream come true" for seniors like him.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To questions by Ms Hany Soh, Mr Christopher de Souza, Mr Seah Kian Peng and Mr Yip Hon Weng, IMDA's SG Digital Office (SDO) was established at the start of the pandemic to provide digital training to seniors in areas like digital services, e-payment and cybersecurity.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Much of this involves one-on-one coaching or small group learning in community spaces where seniors are comfortable.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To date, SDO's Digital Ambassadors have trained more than 210,000 seniors to use smartphones for basic tasks and daily needs.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: By now, many seniors in the heartlands recognise our Digital Ambassadors as "the friendly people in purple shirts".

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since this January, SDO has also worked with the PA's Active Ageing Council to create digital support groups promoting peer learning among our seniors.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To Mr Gerald Giam's question, the Government will be planning for more ServiceSG touchpoints in tandem with demand.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the meantime, the SDOs, our community centres (CCs) as well as libraries do provide basic support.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Yip's example also shows how our libraries are equipping Singaporeans with digital skills.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under NLB's Libraries and Archives Blueprint 2025 (LAB25), libraries will work more closely with leading tech companies to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the inaugural ExperienceIT showcase at the full opening of the Punggol Regional Library later this year, Amazon Web Services will help put together an experiential exhibit introducing visitors to machine learning and artificial intelligence.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This collaborative approach is a consistent thread in our efforts to uplift digital skills.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ms Jessica Tan and Ms Rahayu Mahzam have asked how we are enhancing the Digital for Life movement (DfL).

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is now growing momentum among DfL partners to introduce new programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, Microsoft will offer classes to expose children from low-income families to topics such as Internet of Things (IoT) and Mixed Reality.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As the DfL movement gathers pace, MCI is conducting a series of Forward SG engagements with people, private and public (3P) sector partners to target specific areas of need.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the next phase of engagements, we will focus on topics such as parenting in a digital age and enhancing user experience in digital Government services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, let me now turn to safety and security.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: According to Microsoft's 2023 Global Online Safety Survey, 77% of Singaporeans have experienced at least one online risk in the past year.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the Committee of Supply (COS) debate for the Ministry for Home Affairs (MHA), I shared plans to introduce an Online Criminal Harms Act.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This builds on the Online Safety (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill, which was passed in Parliament last November and came into force recently.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At last year's debate, I explained that the change in law was to enable the introduction of a code of practice for social media services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: IMDA has been engaging industry partners to finalise this code and expects it to be implemented by the second half of the year.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In debating the Bill, I also indicated that we would look beyond social media services to other widely used online communications services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: App stores may carry apps with harmful content, especially for children.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This could include content depicting explicit sexual activities or inciting violence.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As with social media services, app stores should be expected to have systems and processes in place to deal with harmful content.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The new code will take time to be developed and involve industry engagement.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will work out the details and update Members in due course.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the debate on the Bill, there was also strong interest from members for MCI to look into online games.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When the new Code for App Stores is introduced, the risks of exposure to harmful content through games on these stores will be curtailed.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Apps with egregious content may also become unavailable for download.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But games may also be accessed through platforms other than app stores.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will have to study how to deal with this.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A possible measure is to introduce a classification scheme for online games, much as we already do for video games.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will clarify the age-appropriateness of games and help parents exercise better supervision over their children's online gaming.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will work towards these moves over the next 12 to 18 months.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have also started a detailed landscape survey on online gaming to assess if more can be done, for example, to reduce the risk of cyber addiction, which Ms Hany Soh was very concerned about.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This survey is necessary because there is no international consensus on the nature of the problem or the effectiveness of measures.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The concerns in Singapore are also not fully understood.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A survey covering both parents and children will allow us to better understand the issues and shape our response.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This may include working with the people sector to support the vulnerable groups which Mr Baey Yam Keng had identified.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The survey will examine exposure of children to unwanted interactions and inappropriate content on gaming platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will also examine the social and psychological impacts of gaming, extending beyond problematic content.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This requires extensive work and we will do our best to be timely.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Cybersecurity has become a crucial aspect of national security, especially for a country as digitally connected as Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: During last year's debate, I announced that the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA) was reviewing the Cybersecurity Act, which only came into effect in 2018.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since then, CSA has held discussions with its stakeholders, including owners of Critical Information Infrastructure (CII).

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have also engaged trade associations and key industry players.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have made good progress and will start formal industry consultations next month.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: One area under review is how we will adapt our regulatory framework to allow the safe and secure use of virtualised systems beyond CII.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As this is a new area, our discussions with the industry will be important in ensuring that our regulations remain effective.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With increasing industry digitalisation, demand for cybersecurity services has been growing domestically and overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: By now, Members are all aware of seminal developments in AI, including tools like ChatGPT.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While AI brings many benefits, it also brings risks we must mitigate.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is important because AI is increasingly commonplace.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members will recall that in 2019, Singapore launched a Model AI Governance Framework.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will build on these initiatives to strengthen the guardrails that ensure responsible AI development and deployment.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The first is on the use of personal data in AI systems.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will encourage AI users to abide by standards of transparency and explainability so that customers will know when and how AI is being used to process their personal data.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It will also contain best practices on how industry can use personal data to train, test and monitor AI systems.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will set out clear actionable standards for social media services and companies whose products interface with children.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are many more questions about AI that deserve our attention.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members will recall that Open Government Products (OGP) has integrated ChatGPT into Microsoft Word and plans to trial its use among some civil servants.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As more use cases are developed, we will monitor developments to support AI innovation whilst protecting our people.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Emergent technologies that are immersive, decentralised and anonymous, including the metaverse and Web 3.0, could also introduce new types of online risks.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will continue to review our measures to keep in step with technological trends.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will now turn to the third theme of my speech – promoting trust to build social resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To withstand online misinformation, Singaporeans must have trusted and easily accessible sources of information.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In their absence, we cannot assume that our society will hold together.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A citizenry that is informed and information-literate helps to strengthen social resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a key reason for supporting our Public Service media.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To Ms Jessica Tan's question, our local media's digital capabilities have strengthened considerably in the last few years.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To grow online outreach, especially to the young, they have used digital technologies to tell stories in innovative ways.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, Mediacorp has used augmented reality in its coverage of the Russian-Ukraine war.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The Straits Times has used interactive graphics to report on how our HDB flats have changed over the decades and the impact of rising sea levels on our shoreline.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some of these efforts have won international acclaim.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our vernacular media are also making efforts to go where audiences are.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, Mediacorp has launched a digital-first Chinese-language debate programme, “Frontline Connects” or《前线开讲》 that caters primarily to younger audiences online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Berita Harian has produced podcasts discussing social and geopolitical issues, and Tamil Murasu is on track to launch its mobile app this year.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These efforts have paid off especially with younger viewers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: That said, our media has lots more to do.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Singaporeans’ news consumption habits continue to evolve, both SPH Media Trust (SMT) and Mediacorp will have to continue demonstrating progress.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: True transformation will not come just through new technologies but from mindset changes.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Journalists will need to develop new skills and have the support of management in this process.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The road ahead is long and difficult, and we should not underestimate the effort required.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When it comes to promoting information literacy, the National Library Board (NLB) also plays a critical role.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To questions by Ms Tin Pei Ling, since 2013, NLB’s flagship information literacy programme, SURE, has been helping citizens navigate our dense information landscape.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Complementing these efforts, NLB launched the “Read to be SURE” campaign in November 2021 to further promote critical thinking.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The campaign helps Singaporeans hear from different voices on topical issues such as cryptocurrency or gender equality.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Since inception, it has garnered over 220,000 engagements.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Chairman, let me conclude by touching on the international significance of our efforts in digital.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, Singapore is considered one of the leading countries in digital developments, at the frontier of digital infrastructure and regulation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Chairman, MCI wants to empower every Singaporean to thrive in our digital future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In my speech, I will explain two ways in which we are laying the foundations to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: One, by investing in the underlying digital infrastructure to connect all of us and power the digital services and products we use; and two, by building up strong research and innovation capabilities to create new value from emerging technologies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Infrastructure and innovation form the basis for our continued access to quality digital services and content.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For businesses, these allow them to connect to more customers, raise productivity and generate new business value.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our work in these areas is therefore never quite done.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We need to build on our progress, adapt and invest in the future as technology and the world around us and our people’s needs change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: With this in mind, we continue to enhance Singapore’s digital infrastructure to not only meet current demands for speed, capacity and reliability, but to cater for anticipated needs and reap future benefits as technology and the use cases evolve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Understanding future demand will help us make calculated bets as we invest in Singapore’s digital infrastructure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is not always straightforward as technology advances in disruptive and non-linear ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have had to carefully assess technological developments, actively consult the industry and boldly imagine the use cases that consumers and industry would participate in and want to experience here.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The development of our nationwide fibre broadband network (NBN) is a good example of such a calculated, future-oriented bet to build digital infrastructure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: When we made the decision to develop the NBN back in the mid-2000s, most people were comfortable with the 30 megabits per second speed that our copper-based infrastructure already provided.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It was more than sufficient for browsing the web, checking your emails.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Holding virtual conferences and lessons over platforms like Zoom or streaming media content over services like Netflix were not common as they are today, almost 20 years since we began our NBN journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
